It is interesting to contemplate an entangled bank, clothed with many plants of many kinds, with birds singing on the bushes, with various insects flitting about, and with worms crawling through the damp earth, and to reflect that these elaborately constructed forms, so different from each other, and dependent on each other in so complex a manner, have all been produced by laws acting around us. These laws, taken in the largest sense, being Growth with Reproduction; Inheritance which is almost implied by reproduction; Variability from the indirect and direct action of the external conditions of life, and from use and disuse; a Ratio of Increase so high as to lead to a Struggle for Life, and as a consequence to Natural Selection, entailing Divergence of Character and the Extinction of less-improved forms. Thus, from the war of nature, from famine and death, the most exalted object which we are capable of conceiving, namely, the production of the higher animals, directly follows. There is grandeur in this view of life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one; and that, whilst this planet has gone cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity, from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.
</passage>

response.text: It's worth pausing to look closely at a tangled hillside covered with all sorts of plants, alive with birds singing in the shrubs, insects darting here and there, and worms working their way through the moist soil — and to realize that these intricate creatures, so unlike one another and so tightly bound together in their dependence on each other, all came into being through forces still operating today. Broadly speaking, those forces are: growth and reproduction; inheritance, which reproduction almost guarantees; variation, arising both indirectly and directly from environmental conditions and from the use or disuse of body parts; a rate of reproduction so rapid that it triggers a struggle for survival, which in turn brings about natural selection — and with it, the branching apart of species and the dying-out of forms that fail to keep pace. So it is that from nature's conflict, from hunger and death, comes the loftiest outcome imaginable: the emergence of higher forms of animal life. There is something magnificent in this way of seeing life — with all its varied capacities — as having been breathed originally into one form or a handful of forms; and in recognizing that even as this planet has kept turning through its cycles under gravity's unchanging pull, life has been unfolding from such a humble start into an endless array of forms, each more beautiful and remarkable than the last, and that this unfolding continues even now.
